3 May–June of Year 6 — NGRT administered in primary After SATs, pupils sit the NGRT in their own primary school over a three-week window. All diagnostic reading data is available to secondary teams by mid-June — giving schools the summer to plan targeted support before September.

The timing of the NGRT is a deliberate design choice: by running it after SATs, the test does not add pressure to an already high-stakes period, yet the three-week window ensures results land with secondary schools while there is still time to act. b4decd70f7.q: What foundational principle should underpin data management systems in schools?

f: Every grade entered into a school's data system must connect directly to the curriculum — each mark should represent specific knowledge and skills a pupil has actually attained. Without curriculum mapping by teachers, grades become meaningless numbers with no real diagnostic value, making it impossible to use data effectively for intervention or learning improvement.

The challenge is straightforward but often overlooked. Teachers across different subjects frequently record grades without anchoring them to any shared framework. One teacher's "7" may reflect mastery of a skill, while another's "7" might reflect something entirely different — or nothing precise at all. This inconsistency doesn't just create confusion; it renders the entire data system useless for the school's core mission: understanding what pupils know and don't know.

Curriculum mapping is the solution. Once teachers have invested the time to align their grading rubrics with actual curriculum standards — mapping each grade band to specific attainments — the system runs reliably for years forward . The initial work is substantial, but the payoff is durability and consistency. From that point on, every grade carries genuine meaning, and data becomes actionable.
Why grades without curriculum alignment fail schools

When grades live disconnected from curriculum standards, teachers can't reliably track pupil progress, and school leaders can't identify systemic learning gaps. A number in a box tells you almost nothing without knowing what skill or knowledge it represents. Two classes with identical average scores might have vastly different underlying learning profiles — one class strong in application, the other strong in factual recall — but the raw numbers hide that difference.

As Becky Sinjin explains in her work with schools on data strategy , this is where many data management systems break down. Teachers are diligent; they record grades conscientiously. But without a shared map back to the curriculum, the data tells no coherent story. Interventions end up unfocused, and it becomes impossible to measure whether teaching changes have actually worked.

The right choice depends on whether the system delivers the analysis teachers actually need, whether data entry feels manageable for staff, and whether reports are easily accessible across devices like tablets or computers.

Each assessment tracking system comes with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Rather than searching for a single superior solution, schools should focus on understanding which system aligns with their operational priorities and pedagogical goals. As Becky Sinjin explains in the episode , the question isn't which system is universally better, but which one serves your school's particular context.
What to evaluate when selecting a tracking system

Start by examining what analysis and reporting the system can actually provide . Does it generate the specific insights your school needs to understand student progress and inform teaching decisions? Different systems excel at different types of data visualization and analysis, so clarifying your school's priority questions is essential.

Data entry experience matters significantly. Staff comfort with the interface directly affects adoption and consistency—if teachers find data entry cumbersome, the system's value diminishes. Similarly, ensure that accessing reports works the way your teachers prefer, whether that's through simple button clicks, visual graphs, or detailed tables.

Device accessibility is often overlooked but critical in modern schools. The system should work seamlessly across multiple devices including tablets, laptops, and desktop computers , allowing teachers to enter and review data from wherever they are working in the school. This flexibility reflects how teaching and data management actually happen in practice, rather than forcing staff to work only at a central location.

342ea62b21.q: What are the primary challenges mathematics teachers and leaders face in UK schools today?
342ea62b21.a: Andy Small identified multiple challenges: budgeting limitations, significant disparities in staff confidence and experience among teaching staff, with three in ten teachers confessing to feeling anxious about solving math problems in front of classes. Additional challenges include school finance constraints, ongoing attendance difficulties especially in secondary schools where students miss important content, a dense maths curriculum, increasingly complex student needs, limited availability of high-quality maths CPD, and overall time pressures on teachers and leaders.

f: The obstacles are concrete and interconnected: three in ten UK teachers report feeling anxious about solving maths problems in front of their classes , while schools battle budgeting constraints, uneven staff expertise, chronic student absences, overcrowded curricula, and a critical shortage of high-quality professional development. These pressures compound on leaders tasked with managing inconsistent confidence across their teams while meeting increasingly complex student needs.

Budgeting limitations sit at the foundation of nearly every challenge facing maths departments. Schools lack resources to recruit specialists or invest in targeted professional development—a particularly acute problem when many qualified mathematicians choose lucrative careers in the private sector instead of teaching.

Staff experience and confidence are deeply fragmented. Significant disparities exist between teachers , with some feeling equipped to deliver rigorous maths instruction while others struggle with basic problem-solving confidence. This inconsistency creates a ripple effect: students receive uneven quality of teaching depending on which class they're assigned to, and leaders must navigate these dynamics while keeping morale intact.

As Andy Small explains in the episode , student attendance patterns—especially in secondary schools—create cascading learning gaps. When pupils miss sessions, they fall behind on cumulative content they cannot easily recover without targeted intervention.

The curriculum itself presents a structural burden. A dense maths syllabus leaves little room for flexibility, remediation, or deep consolidation of foundational concepts, forcing teachers to move forward regardless of readiness levels across their classes.

Time scarcity compounds every other pressure. Teachers and leaders juggle marking, planning, data management, pastoral duties, and compliance work—leaving minimal space for the collaborative reflection and peer learning that could build collective expertise. Limited availability of high-quality CPD means professional growth often falls to individual initiative rather than systemic support, a challenge Small has explored in depth throughout his years as a maths leader.

On the other, teachers require reliable data that supports informed decision-making, especially in contexts where staff confidence in mathematics varies widely across schools .

The adaptive approach is central to achieving this balance. Rather than presenting a fixed sequence of questions to all test-takers, the test dynamically adjusts difficulty in response to learner performance , ensuring that struggling students receive scaffolding while those excelling encounter genuine challenge. For students finding mathematics challenging, this tailored approach reduces unnecessary frustration , while more confident mathematicians encounter appropriate stretch. The test itself takes between 45 and 60 minutes per learner to administer.

This granularity of data, available almost instantly after completion, transforms the assessment from a summative endpoint into a diagnostic tool for the next teaching sequence.

This isn't simply about long hours. Teachers describe being asked to do more with less: larger classes, fewer support staff, rising pastoral needs, and compliance demands that seem to multiply each term. The workload issue doesn't sit in isolation — it feeds directly into whether educators consider leaving the profession entirely.

What once looked like a lifelong career path now stretches across far shorter tenures.

The shift is striking when measured against living memory. Teachers who entered the profession decades ago often recall their colleagues as fixtures in schools—professionals who taught multiple generations of families and remained until retirement. The damage begins early. Training cohorts are halved before graduation, and many who do graduate never make it to their second year. The profession is haemorrhaging talent before teachers have even begun their careers in earnest.
From pipelines to leaks: the exodus at every stage

As the podcast reveals , 61% of nearly 7,000 respondents to the TES report said their workload is simply not manageable.
